column1: # Published manuscript scans Milah offers for transcription.
# One row per manuscript, tab-separated. Only `url` is required: everything else
# is read from the holding library's own record. Blank lines and lines opening
# with # are ignored, so a manuscript can be annotated with why it is here.
# url    the address as copied from the library's viewer
# title  overrides the library's own title, which sometimes names a whole codex
#        where only a part of it is being transcribed
# book   the OSIS book code, where the scan is of one book; only used to group
#        the list, and empty for a codex covering many
# width  pixels wide to request, default 1024. Honoured only where the library
#        lets a size be asked for: Cambridge serves any width but caps delivery
#        at 2000, while OPenn publishes fixed derivatives and chooses for you.
# folios the part of a codex this row offers, as two of the labels the library
#        itself uses, written 1r..21v. Endpoints are found by position in the
#        page list, never by arithmetic on the folio number: Cambridge's first
#        image is the front cover, so 1r is image 3 in this codex and image
#        something else in the next. Written with .. rather than a hyphen,
#        because OPenn labels endleaves i-r, where the hyphen is part of the
#        label. Empty is the whole codex, which is what every row was before
#        this column existed.
# shelfmark  overrides a record that states none. A bare IIIF manifest carries
#        no shelfmark at all, and it is what tells two manuscripts of the same
#        book apart — and what the picker heads a manuscript's books with.
# licence  the terms, where the library states them somewhere a IIIF manifest
#        has no field for: the Bodleian puts them in its attribution line and
#        leaves `license` unset. Copy what the library says. It is not a place
#        to decide what terms a scan ought to have — a scan whose terms are
#        unclear is one nobody may use, and inventing them does not change that.
# Rows may name one address as often as they like: the library's record is read
# once per run and each row takes its own slice of it.
# Titles here are the book alone, not "Mark (Cambridge, MS Oo.1.32)": the
# shelfmark is a field of its own and the picker shows it above the books it
# holds, so naming the manuscript again in every title prints it twice.
# Regenerate after editing:  python src/build_scan_manifest.py

column1: # Not here, and why — so that nobody spends an afternoon rediscovering it.
# British Library Add MS 26964 is the best witness and is out of copyright, but
# the British Library has served no manuscript since the 2023 cyberattack: its
# IIIF endpoint does not resolve and its catalogue answers 500. Bodleian MS.
# Michael 119 is not digitised at all. Leiden's Even Bohan is Or. 4766 (Warner
# 28), not the Or. 4728 some lists give — that is a translation of al-Zahrawi's
# surgery by Shem Tov ben Isaac of Tortosa, a different man — and its manifest
# is valid but carries no images. JTS MS. 2426 is catalogued but has no public
# IIIF endpoint.
# Two further copies, both with terms weaker than the Bodleian's. What each
# library states is recorded verbatim below, restrictions included: the licence
# column says what a library says, and neither of these says a scan may be
# reused. A transcriber reading either entry is told so before opening it.
# Plut. 2.17 was copied in Tortona in 1385 and is the oldest of them, rated by
# Niclós above the base text of Howard's edition. Its record states an access
# status and no terms of reuse at all.
https://cdm21059.contentdm.oclc.org/iiif/plutei:318709/manifest.json
column2: Even Bohan (Shem Tov's Hebrew Matthew), copied 1385
column7: Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana. Diritti di accesso: Pubblico. The library states an access status and no terms of reuse.

column1: # Ascribed rather than named: the manuscript is certainly a Hebrew Matthew — Mt
